Held at the Presidential Villa, Abuja, on November 19 and 20, the summit brought together government officials, state governors, sports administrators, coaches, investors and development partners to address the structural challenges undermining grassroots sports development.
With the theme, “Creating a New Pathway for Sustainable Grassroots Sports Development in Nigeria” , the gathering sought to address a long-standing contradiction in Nigerian sports: the country has an abundance of raw talent but lacks the facilities, funding and institutional structures required to identify, nurture and sustain it.
The message from President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, represented by Secretary to the Government of the Federation, Senator George Akume, was unequivocal: Nigeria must move beyond celebrating sporting talent and begin building the structures that will consistently produce champions.
In his address, Tinubu outlined eight priorities for repositioning grassroots sports: sustainable development programmes across the federation, rehabilitation of community sports facilities, national talent identification, improved funding, coaches’ development, integration of sports into schools, greater inclusion and sports entrepreneurship.
He called for grassroots sports structures to be established and strengthened across the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory, stressing that the journey to becoming an Olympic or world champion begins in local communities.
The President also advocated the integration of sports into the school curriculum, arguing that schools must become critical centres for discovering and nurturing young talents.
Particular emphasis was placed on inclusion, with a call for greater opportunities for girls, persons with disabilities and children from underserved communities.
Tinubu maintained that poverty, geographical location and social circumstances should not prevent talented Nigerians from pursuing sporting careers.
The challenge, however, is translating these priorities into a sustainable system that reaches the 774 local government areas, where many promising athletes remain undiscovered and underdeveloped.
Funding emerged as one of the most pressing issues at the summit, with Director-General of the National Institute for Sports, Hon. Philip Shaibu, renewing calls for dedicated sports trust funds at federal and state levels.
The proposed funds would pool resources from government agencies, corporate organisations and philanthropic individuals to provide a more reliable financing framework for sports development.
The proposal reflects growing recognition that annual government budgetary allocations alone cannot adequately sustain grassroots sports programmes, maintain facilities and support talent development across the country.

A dedicated funding structure, if properly established and managed, could provide the financial consistency required to move grassroots sports beyond occasional government interventions.
The summit’s organisers were equally conscious of the danger of allowing the gathering to become another exercise in policy declarations without measurable outcomes.
Hon. Adeyinka Adeboye, Senior Special Assistant to the President on Grassroots Sports Development and convener of the summit, said the objective was to secure practical recommendations, measurable commitments and partnerships capable of delivering lasting results.
“We are not gathering simply to deliver speeches,” Adeboye said, emphasising the need for decisions that would continue to produce results long after the summit.
He also stressed that grassroots sports development could not be achieved from Abuja alone, noting that the talents Nigeria seeks are scattered across schools, villages and communities.
According to him, state governments, local government authorities, schools, sports federations and private organisations must take greater responsibility for investing in facilities, talent identification and training programmes.
Former Lagos State Governor and former Minister of Works, Babatunde Raji Fashola, reinforced the message, warning that the country could not afford another summit whose resolutions would end with the closing ceremony.
“This must not be another talk show. We must go beyond this meeting to get the job done,” Fashola said.
He expressed concern over the postponement of the 2026 National Sports Festival in Enugu to May 2027, arguing that repeated changes to major sporting events disrupt athletes’ preparations, undermine administrative planning and weaken sponsors’ confidence.
Fashola advocated a coordinated national sports calendar linking school competitions, local government games, university championships and national festivals with continental and international events.
He argued that a predictable competition structure would strengthen talent identification and provide athletes with a clear progression pathway from grassroots participation to elite competition.
He also challenged the country to encourage local production of sports equipment, proposing tax incentives to attract corporate investment and support the development of a domestic sports manufacturing industry.
Beyond the policy discussions and funding proposals, the summit also brought attention to the people whose contributions often go unnoticed in Nigeria’s sporting ecosystem: grassroots coaches and talent developers.
Hon. Frank Ilaboya, Special Adviser on Grassroots Sports Mobilisation to the Edo State Governor, particularly commended a presentation by Chief Yemi Idowu, which advocated a recognition and reward system for grassroots coaches and other stakeholders who identify and nurture young athletes.
Ilaboya described the proposal as an important contribution to the discussion, noting that coaches who work at the formative stages of athletes’ careers deserve institutional recognition and adequate support.
“Chief Idowu’s paper was an opener because he advocated for due recognition for those who nurtured these young talents to stardom,” he said.
He expressed optimism that implementing even half of the recommendations from the summit could significantly improve grassroots sports development in Nigeria.
His remarks, however, highlighted a fundamental concern: the people responsible for discovering and developing talent must not be left out of the reforms being proposed.
Across many communities, grassroots coaches operate with limited equipment, inadequate facilities and little or no financial support. Yet, they remain the first point of contact for countless athletes who eventually represent the country.
The Nigerian Economic Summit Group’s involvement as technical partner also provided an opportunity to develop a more structured approach to implementing the summit’s recommendations.
However, the challenge remains ensuring that the proposed frameworks translate into tangible support for coaches, athletes and communities, rather than becoming another layer of administrative commitments.
Ultimately, the significance of the summit will not be determined by the number of dignitaries who attended or the quality of speeches delivered, but by the progress recorded in the months ahead.
Three areas will be particularly important in assessing whether the gathering has laid the foundation for meaningful reform.
First is the proposed sports trust fund. Moving the initiative from advocacy to an operational funding structure, supported by clear accountability measures, would provide a significant boost to grassroots development.
Such a framework must ensure that resources reach athletes, coaches, schools and community sports programmes instead of being consumed by administrative costs.
Second is the establishment of a predictable national sports calendar. Without regular competitions at school, local government, state and national levels, talent identification will remain largely dependent on chance.
A properly coordinated calendar would provide young athletes with regular opportunities to compete, improve and progress through the sporting system.
Third is the welfare and professional development of grassroots coaches. Beyond recognition, they need access to certification programmes, regular training, financial incentives and institutional support.
A sustainable grassroots system cannot be built on the sacrifices of unpaid coaches whose commitment often keeps community sports programmes alive.
Tinubu also presented sports as an economic opportunity capable of generating employment in coaching, sports science, facility management, journalism, tourism and other related industries.
He urged private investors to look beyond the traditional perception of sports as recreation and recognise its potential as a viable sector for investment and job creation.
That economic argument could prove important in attracting private capital and establishing partnerships that reduce the dependence of grassroots sports on government funding.
But the ultimate measure of success will be whether these commitments reach beyond the Presidential Villa.
For the coach working with limited resources in Ilorin or Yenagoa, the teenager struggling to afford transportation to a trial, or the promising athlete training on an abandoned community pitch, the value of the summit will be determined by what changes in their daily reality.
Nigeria has never been short of sporting talent. What it has lacked is a dependable system to discover, develop and retain that talent.
The Abuja summit has outlined a new direction through its eight-point agenda and funding proposals. The real challenge now is to turn those promises into functioning programmes across the country’s 774 local government areas.
